Guide

When a child is ill

Familiar food, enough fluid, and the usual milk. A sick day is a bad day to diagnose an allergy or to start a new one.

Findings

Fluids and milk come before a perfect menu. Small, familiar meals are enough. Do not fast a young child.
Do not introduce a new allergen during an illness. A rash or a vomit on that day is impossible to interpret.
Know the signs that need a clinician the same day. Poor urine output, a sunken fontanelle, blood in the stool, unusual sleepiness, or hard breathing are not home observations to sit on.

Feed the illness, gently

Appetite falls with fever and with a sore mouth. Breast milk or formula continues. Offer smaller amounts of foods the child already likes. Yogurt, fruit, a plain porridge, or a broth you have not salted are enough. Forcing a balanced plate onto a nauseated child earns a food aversion.

Oral rehydration solution is the right tool for vomiting or diarrhoea when milk alone is not keeping up. A health visitor can walk you through it. Sugary juice is a poor substitute and can worsen diarrhoea.

Leave experiments for a well week

Illness changes skin and stools. A new food on the same day creates a false allergy story and a food the family then avoids for years. Wait until the child is well, then return to the introduction plan.

Teething and illness get blamed for each other. A fever that is more than a small rise, or a child who is distinctly unwell, is not explained by a tooth. Have them seen.

When to call

Call the same day if the child is under three months with a fever, is unusually floppy or hard to wake, is breathing with effort, has blood in vomit or stool, or is not passing urine. Those are the situations where food advice is irrelevant.

After antibiotics, the diet does not need a special cleanse. Ordinary food, including yogurt if they like it, is fine. Probiotic products are optional and are not a required part of recovery.
